comment.value:
This paper addresses the underexplored problem of Virtual Footwear Try-On, introducing both a new dataset and a novel architecture tailored to the unique challenges of footwear try-on, including data scarcity, viewpoint misalignment, and background-induced color distortion. The proposed dual-stream DiT framework leverages multi-view conditioning with 3D rotary position embeddings and a layered attention mechanism to decouple shoe appearance from environmental effects while preserving texture detail. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in fidelity and robustness compared to existing methods.

All four reviewers rated the paper as borderline accept. Reviewers NYQo, Bocv find that the scope of validation could be broader, particularly including results on external real-world data. Reviewer Bocv finds the performance limitations remain for style variations and in handling the sock region. Overall, reviewers acknowledged that while the contributions are solid, the paper would benefit from further refinement and expanded validation.

The reviewers converge on a borderline accept rating, emphasizing that the paper makes a novel and timely contribution by opening up a new subfield with both a benchmark dataset and a tailored architecture. While there are valid concerns regarding the scope of evaluation and certain qualitative limitations, these do not outweigh the significance of releasing a dedicated dataset and establishing a baseline framework. Thus, the AC recommends accept.

We express profound appreciation for your recognition of our supplementary ablation studies – your expert insights have been instrumental in enhancing the methodological rigor of our experimental section. This engagement has significantly fortified the robustness of our contribution. Should any additional questions arise, we enthusiastically welcome further discussion of this work. We remain grateful for your guidance throughout this review process.

1. **Regarding shoe series style variations**:  
Unfortunately, due to NeurIPS 2025's PDF submission restrictions, we cannot provide more cases in the rebuttal phase. Some examples of shoe series style variations that may be of interest are in rows 4-6 in Fig. 6 in the Appendix PDF. Intra-series style variations are not chanllenges for ShoeFit. In fact, intra-series style variations are easier than cross-category try-ons.

---

2. **Regarding out-of-distribution testing**:  
We fully concur that evaluating on out-of-distribution (OOD) examples would strengthen the robustness validation of our method. As rightfully noted in your Strengths assessment, our research **pioneers the VFTON task** and introduces **the first dedicated footwear dataset** (MVShoes). This pioneering status presents a fundamental constraint: **no established OOD benchmark exists for footwear try-on to date**. 

   Moreover, MVShoes inherently incorporates significant distributional diversity through:
   - **Real-world environmental variation**: Natural outdoor lighting conditions (e.g., sunlight, shadows) contrasting with controlled indoor settings of VITON-HD, DressCode, MV-VTON and Robust-MVTON
   - **Comprehensive coverage**: As detailed in Section 3.2, the dataset spans diverse footwear categories (athletic, formal, boots) and challenging try-on scenarios

   Given these constraints, constructing a formally comparable OOD benchmark remains currently infeasible. Nevertheless, we conducted a preliminary robustness evaluation using 20 **stylistically divergent samples** from anime and video game sources (distinct distribution from MVShoes). Key findings:
   - Our method achieved **85% human-evaluated success rate** (defined as plausible texture preservation and structural integrity)
   - CAT-VTON baseline attained only **60% success rate** under identical evaluation criteria
   - Failure cases primarily involved extreme stylistic exaggerations (e.g., oversized fantasy elements)

   We will include these exploratory cases in the Appendix of our revised manuscript, providing initial evidence of cross-distribution robustness while acknowledging the need for more formal OOD benchmarks as the field matures.

   Upon thorough comparison with seminal works in try-on literature, we note that the highly influential VITON-HD [1] - which share similar data contribution to our study - similarly reports only in-distribution results without cross-dataset or other real-world testing, due to the same reason of OOD benchmark absence to ours. While MVShoes (7,305 triplets) is smaller than VITON-HD (13,679 images), the scale difference remains under 2×. 

   We respectfully request consideration as the inaugural study in this nascent domain. We are committed to expanding MVShoes through additional data collection and welcome future benchmarking against emerging following datasets.

---

Thank you for your insightful review! We would be pleased to engage in further discussion to elaborate on any points of interest or concern regarding our ShoeFit and VFTON.

---
**Reference**  
[1] VITON-HD: High-Resolution Virtual Try-On via Misalignment-Aware Normalization

1. **Regarding the challenge discussion and MV-VTON comparison**:  
   We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments regarding the relative challenges of VFTON versus VTON. We respectfully concur that VFTON should not be characterized as inherently more challenging than VTON. However, VFTON presents **distinct research difficulties** that differ in focus from those in VTON, explaining why conventional VTON methods underperform on MVShoes, as demonstrated in Figure 5 (main paper) and Appendix Figure 5.

   Regarding MV-VTON and Robust-MVTON, we note significant differences in both input requirements and environmental conditions:
   - **Input perspective**: MV-VTON/Robust-MVTON utilize fixed frontal and dorsal garment views, while VFTON requires arbitrary-perspective shoe views due to footwear's 3D nature
   - **Material challenges**: Footwear introduces unique complexities like reflective surfaces and rigid structures absent in garment try-on
   - **Environmental diversity**: MVShoes captures real-world scenarios with natural outdoor lighting, contrasting with the controlled indoor environments of VITON-HD, DressCode, MV-VTON and Robust-MVTON

   The value of this novel task lies not in perceived difficulty but in its strong **practical applicability** for e-commerce, **community impact** through dataset creation, and **research inspiration** for 3D-aware try-on systems. We believe VFTON offers significant real-world utility and represents an unexplored research direction.

   We agree this distinction merits clearer exposition and will incorporate a detailed comparative analysis of task-specific challenges in our revision. We are grateful for your constructive suggestions, which have significantly helped refine our positioning of VFTON within the virtual try-on research landscape.

---

2. **Regarding the inflation phenomenon in sports footwear**:  
   Yes, the volumetric expansion observed in athletic footwear during try-on is a natural characteristic. We appreciate your valuable and meticulous feedback, which prompted us to reexamine our dataset. We confirmed that such footwear features stiff tongues that rise up when worn, resulting in slight volumetric inflation. As illustrated in Figure 5(3):  
   - Column 2 shows the tongue positioned inside the shoe  
   - Column 3 demonstrates the tongue visibly rise up when worn, which expand the footwear.

   This inflation phenomenon occurs probabilistically in ground-truth pairs, as evidenced in Figure 1(a)(3) where column 2 exhibits a marginally thicker shoe profile.  

   It's worth to mention that as the pioneering work in this domain, our method substantially outperforms existing baselines (Figure 5, main paper; Appendix Figure 5), as recognized by all reviewers. Baseline methods frequently fail to preserve structural integrity, producing noticeably distorted textures - findings that robustly validate our technical performance. 

   We are grateful for your constructive advice, and will discuss the inflation phenomenon in the Appendix of our revision version. Thank you!

---

# Response to Reviewer B4SC

We sincerely thank you for your recognition of our work's novel task, dataset contribution, and model performance. Your feedback—particularly the suggestion to supplement ablation experiments—has significantly enhanced the rigor of our paper. We appreciate your expertise in this field and meticulous review. Please rest assured that the **MVShoes dataset will be publicly released upon paper acceptance**, which we consider a major contribution of this work. We have conducted all requested experiments and address your concerns as follows:

---

## Weakness 1: Data Processing Improvements

Compared to VTON, our data processing improvements focus on **dwpose preparation** and **mask design** with two key innovations:

### 1. **Pose Estimation for Shoe Try-On**
Traditional open-source pose estimation methods (e.g., OpenPose, DWPose) in VITON pipeline, struggle to capture lower-body/foot poses in VFTON, which often only include partial leg shots or full lower-body views. To address this, we fine-tuned the **dwpose model** on specially collected datasets containing diverse lower-body and close-up leg poses. This enables our model to generate accurate pose descriptions for various leg postures, significantly enhancing its generalization capability for shoe-related applications.

### 2. **Generalizable Foot Mask Design**
Given the diversity of shoe types (e.g., sneakers, boots, sandals) and their varying leg coverage, we propose a **leg-pose-aware mask generation strategy**. Unlike VTON's body-centric masks, our method combines leg pose information with bounding box expansion from shoe detection to create **adaptive masks**. This allows seamless cross-shoe category try-on capabilities—for example, a model wearing long boots or flip-flops can be transformed into sneakers while maintaining anatomical alignment and realistic occlusion. Please refer to the row 1 in Fig.5 of Appendix PDF. This approach lays the foundation for robust, universal shoe try-on systems.

---

## Weakness 2: Multi-View Concatenation

Thank you for your valuable feedback on the **Multi-View Concatenation**. While similar to CAT-VTON in concept, our implementation has distinct objectives and functionalities, with experiment insights:

1. **Insights of viewpoints in VFTON**:  
   We discovered and identified that shoes, as rigid bodies, exhibit **viewpoint misalignment** phenomena. Our contribution lies in introducing **multi-view conditioning** to address this, validating its effectiveness in VFTON generation, which has not been studied and reported in previous try-on works.

2. **Differences from CAT-VTON About Concatenation**:  
   - **CAT-VTON**: CAT-VTON shares a single image-stream for both generation and condition branches, with concatenation occurring between noise and condition features (acting as condition injection).  
   - **ShoeFit**: We employ a **dual image-stream** architecture, separately processing generation and condition branches. Concatenation occurs **within the condition features**, serving as **information supplementation**. 

For details on **3D RoPE**, please refer to **Weakness 4**.

---

## Weakness 3: Ablation Study Clarification

Thank you for your expert insights. We acknowledge the unclear statement in our original ablation study. During the LayeredRefAttention ablation, we replaced it with standard attention layers **without masks**. To validate whether background suppression via simple masking contributes to performance gains, we conducted an additional experiment using standard attention but **masked out product shoe backgrounds** (following the Diptych Prompting you mentioned). 

Due to NeurIPS rebuttal policy, we cannot include visual results but report the quantitative metrics below:

|           Methods                   |       SSIM     |      LPIPS     |      FID     |      KID     |      DISTS      |
|-------------------------------------|----------------|----------------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|
| + D-i-s                             |      0.761     |      0.174     |      21.57   |     1.493    |      0.1038     |
| + D-i-s + standard ATTN (with mask) |      0.756     |      0.181     |      21.70   |     1.698    |      0.1056     |
| + D-i-s + LRA (with mask)           |      0.772     |      0.159     |      21.07   |     0.944    |      0.1059     |

Visually, **simple background masking** exacerbates color deviations, especially for bright, pure colors. As discussed in the paper (Line 205), naive background suppression neglects critical **illumination cues** embedded in product images, which are essential for inferring shoes' intrinsic appearance and texture. This is because product shoe images and shoes on human feet often differ slightly in color **in the trainset** due to **varied lighting conditions** during collection. Removing backgrounds allows the model to freely guess lighting conditions during training, leading to reduced color fidelity.

---

## Weakness 4: 3D RoPE Ablation

Thank you for your suggestion. We have supplemented an ablation study on **3D RoPE**'s impact as following: 


|           Methods                   |       SSIM     |      LPIPS     |      FID     |      KID     |      DISTS      |
|-------------------------------------|----------------|----------------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|
| + D-i-s + LRA + MC (w/o 3D RoPE)    |      0.778     |      0.152     |      20.18   |     0.695    |      0.0971     |
| + D-i-s + LRA + MC (Full)           |      0.780     |      0.149     |      20.18   |     0.485    |      0.0941     |

It demonstrates the performance gain we achieved using the proposed RopE without incurring any additional computational overhead.
Your advice is very valuable: **3D RoPE** adds an index-based channel per image, increasing dimensionality but differing from traditional 3D semantics. We will revise the terminology in the revision to avoid ambiguity.

---

## Question 1: Teaser Image Corner Case

The issue in the **second row's final example** in the teaser image is actually caused by **extreme occlusion** and **inpainting mask strategy**, not depth ambiguity or lack of 3D reasoning. Our model is robust to **foot poses** and **inter-shoe distances** due to **separate masking** and **joint inpainting**. Spatially separated, asymmetric, or partially occluded input footwear does not degrade try-on quality, **as demonstrated row 1 of Fig.6 in Appendix PDF, and in rows 2–5 of Fig. 5 (notably the rear shoe in row 4) in main paper**.

In the teaser image's second row, the **extremely small and occluded rear shoe area** led to failure in **keypoint detection** and **shoe Detection**, marking the rear shoe as a background region. Only the front foot area was designated as the inpainting region, resulting in the bad case. We consider this an engineering limitation, resolvable with advancements in segmentation and detection models. We will explicitly discuss such limitations in the revised manuscript. Thanks for your responsible review!

---

We hope these clarifications address your concerns and look forward to your further feedback.

We sincerely thank you for your high recognition of our work's novelty in defining the VFTON task, constructing the MVShoes dataset, and strong paper quality. The **MVShoes dataset will be publicly released once this paper is accepted**. We address your concerns as follows:

---

## Weakness: Contribution Clarification

Thank you for your insightful feedback! As you noted: *"the main contribution of the paper seems to be the MVShoes dataset, this may be acceptable"*. Besides, we emphasize that **our network architecture is also a good contribution**, developed through iterative improvements in VFTON experiments. Key innovations include:

- **Dual-Image-Stream DiT Architecture**: Enables parallel processing of multi-view shoe products and person images.
- **Multi-View Conditioning Mechanism**: Resolves viewpoint misalignment issues inherent in footwear try-on.
- **LayeredRefAttention Module**: Mitigates background-induced color distortion by layer-wise reference attention.

These innovations collectively enable our method to outperform baselines like CatVTON, which lack specialized mechanisms for footwear-specific challenges.

---

## Question 1: Shoe Series Style Variations

Thank you for your suggestion regarding consumer-oriented evaluation scenarios. We think your suggestion is very reasonable. Due to NeurIPS 2025's PDF submission restrictions, please refer to rows 4-6 in Fig.6 in the Appendix PDF about  **try-on visualizations of different styles within the same shoe series**. Your feedback is well-founded, and we observe:

- **Structure requirements**: Trying on shoes with small variations is a less difficult type of try-on, in which case the model is possible to obtain footwear shape hints from the inpainting mask.
- **Texture detail requirements**: Both small- and large-variation scenarios demand similar attention to detail in virtual try-on results, as you noted: *"both scenarios demand high attention to detail in the virtual try-on results"*

While we cannot present intra-series style variations in rebuttal results, please refer to Fig. 5&6 in the Appendix for more generalized cases of our method. Notably, our **unpaired testing protocol** randomly shuffles human-shoe pairs from the diverse MVShoes dataset (covering 20+ shoe categories), resulting in most test cases involving substantial design differences.

---

## Question 2: Sock Generation Behavior

Your meticulous observation reflects your expertise and carefulness as a reviewer. Sock generation depends critically on the **inpainting mask design**:

1. **Mask Strategy**: Following VTON conventions, we use keypoint detection and shoe detection to remove original footwear in person images. This inevitably affects adjacent sock regions.
2. **Case Analysis (Figure 5)**:
   - **Row 1**: Inpainting mask covers most sock area, leaving only a small unchanged top edge. Model generates socks matching the preserved edge color (with minor pattern variations).
   - **Rows 2, 3, 5**: Most socks remain in unchanged regions, preserving input sock appearance.
   - **Row 4**: Nearly all of the sock area under the inpainting mask leads to heel-style sock removal (consistent with high-heel wear habits).
3. **The same as VTON**: Similar phenomena occur in upper-body cloth try-on, where pants shape near the waist often changes when the lower section is in the inpainting region.

In general, **the model generates reasonable images of the sock area inside the inpainting mask that are consistent with the training data distribution**, which generally leads to **harmonious appearance**. In our opinion, for VFTON tasks, preserving original socks is not strictly required. For more controlled sock retention, we recommend exploring **mask-free try-on approaches** like BooW-VTON [1], which avoid inpainting masks to preserve full input sock context.

---

Thank you for your suggestions on paper formatting! We will correct them in the revised version.

---

## References

[1] BooW-VTON: Boosting In-the-Wild Virtual Try-On via Mask-Free Pseudo Data Training 

---


We hope these clarifications address your concerns and look forward to your further feedback.

# Response to Reviewer NYQo

We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our work's significance in the VFTON (Virtual footwear try-on) proposal, dataset contribution, comprehensive experiments, and clear writing style. We are also grateful for your constructive suggestions. Some of the concerns you raised stem from misunderstandings of our work, which we clarify below. Due to the NeurIPS 2025 policy prohibiting PDF attachments, we can only provide textual explanations instead of visual examples.

---

## Question 1.1: Difference between VFTON and VTON

This is a natural thought, reflecting your expertise in the field. While VFTON does not require generating loose, deformable clothing (as shoes are nearly rigid bodies), it introduces unique challenges distinct from VTON. Specifically, **multi-view understanding** is one of the central to VFTON. 

- **Task Alignment**: VTON typically generates front-facing clothed avatars from flat-lay front-view clothing images, involving fixed-perspective, aligned generation. In contrast, footwear try-on requires **arbitrary-perspective generation**, as shown in the multi-view nature of VFTON. 
- **Model Capabilities**: We conducted VTON training previously and observed that pre-trained diffusion models inherently generate realistic fabric folds with consistent lighting even in early stages. This suggests that deformable clothing generation is an emergent capability of such models. However, **spatial reasoning for footwear** is not natively supported. For example, multi-view shoe product images often show different patterns on the outer and inner sides (e.g., Figure 2(a) row 1 column 5). Early-stage VFTON results frequently exhibited flipped inner/outer textures, indicating the need for long-term spatial understanding training.

Thus, while both tasks involve virtual try-on, their technical challenges and focus areas differ, making direct difficulty comparisons inappropriate.

---

## Question 1.2: Dataset Scale of MVShoes

Thank you for your expertise; your comments have been very enlightening, and we're grateful. We acknowledge the current dataset scale limitations and outline the reasons below:

1. **Multi-view Collection Complexity**:  
   - Unlike try-on datasets (e.g., VITON-HD, DressCode) that use single-view clothing-product pairs, MVShoes requires collecting **multi-view shoe product images**. Such data is significantly rarer and more expensive to acquire (only ~25,000 qualified raw shoe product image sets were collected at submission time). Please refer to Fig. 2 in the Appendix PDF.

2. **Strict Data Filtering Pipeline**:  
   - Multi-view shoe images often exhibit content inconsistencies (e.g., same style from the same shops but different color variants), which drastically reduces valid triplet counts after filtering.

3. **In-the-wild Person Images**:  
   - MVShoes includes real-world person images with complex backgrounds, requiring stricter segmentation and attribute extraction compared to clean studio-shot datasets (e.g., VITON-HD, DressCode). Our zero-tolerance policy for "bad cases" further limits sample counts after careful human filtering. Please refer to Fig. 2 in the Appendix PDF.

We will continue expanding MVShoes and plan to open-source more when sufficient scale is achieved, continually contributing to the research community in the future.

---

## Question 2: Visualization Concerns

Thank you for your meticulous and responsible review. We re-examined the ShoeFit results for the cases you mentioned and did not observe shape or material distortions. Could you please clarify the specific aspects of concern? We agree the current dataset size is limited, and our ongoing data collection efforts aim to address this.

---

## Question 3: Public Datasets for VFTON

We appreciate your suggestion and carefully examined the DeepFashion and DeepFashion2 benchmarks. However, as far as we know, we found **no publicly available image pairs** containing both product shoe images and corresponding person images suitable for VFTON. Actually, the lack of public datasets motivated us to create MVShoes, which we consider a major contribution of this work.

---

We hope these clarifications address your concerns and look forward to your further feedback.

summary.value: This paper explores a new task of virtual footwear try-on (VFTON). To address the challenges of data scarcity, viewpoint misalignment, and background-induced color distortion in VFTON, this paper first establishes a new dataset called MVShoes, which comprises 7305 annotated high-resolution image triplets, each containing two product shoe images from different views and a corresponding try-on result, then proposes a new dual-image-stream DiT framework (named ShoeFit) by using Multi-View Conditioning and LayeredRefAttention modules. These modules enhance the fidelity of try-on results by managing complex lighting interactions and preserving high-quality texture details. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments validate the superiority of ShoeFit in generating high-fidelity and robust try-on results.

summary.value: This paper addresses the unique challenges of Virtual Footwear Try-On (VFTON), including data scarcity, viewpoint misalignment, and background-induced color distortion, which differentiate it from garment-based VTON. To tackle these issues, the authors introduce MVShoes, the first large-scale multi-view footwear try-on dataset with 7,305 annotated image triplets. They also propose ShoeFit, a dual-stream DiT-based architecture that incorporates Multi-View Conditioning with 3D Rotary Position Embedding and a LayeredRefAttention module to enhance texture fidelity and reduce environmental interference. The model effectively decouples shoe appearance from background noise and improves rendering quality under real-world conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ShoeFit sets a new benchmark in high-fidelity footwear try-on synthesis.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths
- The most significant strength of this paper lies in the introduction of the MVShoes dataset, which, if released publicly, could catalyze research in the underexplored domain of Virtual Footwear Try-On (VFTON). The lack of publicly available footwear datasets has been a major bottleneck in expanding VTON research beyond garments like tops and bottoms. By providing a high-quality, multi-view dataset, this work opens the door for adapting existing VTON models (e.g., CATVTON) to a new task, potentially establishing VFTON as a standard benchmark in the community.
- The proposed ShoeFit architecture integrates multiple components—such as dual-image streams, multi-view conditioning, and background-aware attention—which collectively contribute to improved realism and robustness in try-on synthesis.

### Weaknesses
- While the dataset itself is valuable, the data processing pipeline lacks technical novelty, appearing to follow conventional VTON data collection and preprocessing practices without introducing new methodologies tailored to footwear-specific challenges.
- The ablation study is insufficiently thorough, making it difficult to isolate the contributions of individual components. For instance, the Multi-View Image Concatenation is directly borrowed from CATVTON and involves simple concatenation without architectural innovation. Similarly, the use of 3D RoPE is somewhat misleading in terminology—it merely adds an index-based channel per image, which may not fully justify the "3D" label and could benefit from clearer naming.
- The LayeredRefAttention module includes a conditional mask mechanism, but it is unclear whether the ablation study isolates the effect of the mask itself versus the attention mechanism. This ambiguity raises questions about whether performance gains stem from the attention design or simply from background suppression via masking, as seen in works like Diptych Prompting [1].
- Additionally, the impact of 3D RoPE is not clearly quantified. A comparison with 2D RoPE (as used in CATVTON) would help clarify whether the proposed positional encoding offers meaningful improvements.

[1] Large-Scale Text-to-Image Model with Inpainting is a Zero-Shot Subject-Driven Image Generator, CVPR 2025


I believe the paper presents a promising direction for expanding the VTON domain into footwear, and the introduction of the MVShoes dataset is a valuable contribution. However, the current version lacks sufficient ablation analysis to convincingly demonstrate the effectiveness of each proposed component. If the authors can provide a more thorough and transparent ablation study—particularly isolating the effects of 3D RoPE, LayeredRefAttention, and the conditional masking mechanism—I would be inclined to raise my score. I look forward to the authors’ response and clarification on these points.

questions.value: One notable failure case appears in the teaser image, specifically in the second row's final example, where the rear shoe is not properly changed in the try-on result. This highlights a critical challenge in VFTON: handling spatially separated footwear, such as when shoes are not symmetrically aligned or are partially occluded. These cases are inherently more difficult due to depth ambiguity, occlusion, and the lack of explicit 3D reasoning in the model. It would be valuable to understand whether such failures are isolated or occur frequently across the dataset, and whether the model is robust to varying foot poses and inter-shoe distances. (It would be better discussing such observations in the limitation part, which is not clearly discussed in the current paper.)

The paper introduces ShoeFit, a framework for virtual footwear try-on (VFTON), addressing key challenges unique to shoes: data scarcity, viewpoint misalignment, and background-induced color distortion. To tackle the lack of realistic datasets, the authors curate MVShoes, a multi-view shoe try-on dataset comprising annotated image triplets, covering various footwear categories and real-world scenes.

At the core of their solution is a dual-image-stream DiT architecture, built upon FLUX.1-Lite, that separates denoising and conditioning to preserve shoe texture fidelity. The method incorporates two key modules: Multi-View Conditioning, using Reference Concatenation and 3D Rotary Position Embeddings to align different shoe perspectives, and LayeredRefAttention, which helps disentangle shoe appearance from environmental lighting and background. Their experiments show that ShoeFit significantly outperforms existing baselines, establishing a new benchmark for future VFTON research.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: 

This paper offers a contribution to the virtual try-on space by zooming into the challenges of virtual footwear try-on (VFTON), which has been largely underserved. The introduction of the MVShoes dataset, with 7305 annotated triplets across multi-view scenes and diverse shoe categories, and the authors have been meticulous in data curation, including pose alignment, background separation, and high-resolution filtering. From a quality standpoint, this dataset sets a strong potential for future work in VFTON.

The proposed ShoeFit model, built upon a dual-image-stream DiT framework, and the architectural decisions such as decoupling conditioning from denoising, using Multi-View Conditioning with 3D RoPE, and introducing LayeredRefAttention, are well motivated and grounded in the unique difficulties of shoes (reflectivity, misalignment, subtle variations). The experiments are well executed, with comprehensive metrics (SSIM, FID, DISTS, etc.) and comparisons to both strong baselines and state-of-the-art models like CatVTON and OOTDiffusion. Ablation studies are also nicely done, showing the incremental value of each module.

Weaknesses: 

While the technical content is strong, the clarity of presentation could be improved in some parts. The paper occasionally leans on heavy architectural jargon (e.g., long sequences explaining attention math) without providing more visual or intuitive explanations, which might make it harder for readers to digest. A clearer visual roadmap, especially of the dual-stream pipeline, would help.

From a significance angle, this is a clear step forward for VFTON, but the broader impact could be more explicitly explored. The work is very tailored to footwear, which limits its generalization to other product categories. It would be good to know whether the architecture can scale or adapt to accessories, or other reflective materials like handbags or sunglasses.

Originality: 

The originality is solid. While it builds on existing diffusion and DiT frameworks, the way it adapts them specifically for VFTON is novel and well justified. Concepts like LayeredRefAttention and multi-view RoPE adaptation are interesting technical contributions.

summary.value: This paper focuses on the task of Virtual Footwear Try-On (VFTON) and introduces MVShoes, a multi-view shoe try-on dataset with 7,305 well-annotated image triplets, covering various footwear categories and challenging try-on scenarios. In addition, the paper proposes a customized dual-image-stream DiT architecture called ShoeFit for generating high-fidelity try-on results. If MVShoes will be released publicly, I believe this work will make a contribution to the field.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Virtual Footwear Try-On (VFTON) is a promising and worthwhile direction to explore.
2. The proposed MVShoes dataset includes human foot images, pose annotations, masks, and multi-view product shoe images, which—if released—would be a valuable contribution to the field.

Weaknesses:
1. The proposed generation method, ShoeFit, appears to lack substantial novelty. However, since the main contribution of the paper seems to be the MVShoes dataset, this may be acceptable.
2. There are questions regarding the virtual try-on methodology, please refer to the “Questions” section.

questions.value:
1. Since Virtual Footwear Try-On is a task closely tied to real-world applications, it’s important to consider actual consumer behavior. In practice, many users prefer to virtually try on different styles within the same shoe series (e.g., Nike Dunk, adidas Ultraboost). These shoes typically share similar geometry but differ in materials, textures, and fine decorative details. The scenarios explored in the paper primarily focus on trying on shoes with substantial variations in style, shape, and color, such as transitioning between sneakers, boots, or high heels, which differs from this specific use case. However, both scenarios demand high attention to detail in the virtual try-on results. I would like to see ShoeFit’s performance on such subtler, yet practically relevant, use cases.

2. It is noted that in Figure 5, the sock regions in the ShoeFit results sometimes differ from those in the input images. This may have undesirable effects—for example, in the first row, the generated socks differ from those in the input, potentially affecting try-on accuracy. However, it might also lead to positive effects in certain cases—for instance, in the fourth row, after trying on high heels, the socks in the result may be replaced by sheer stockings or bare feet. Is the change in socks controllable?

1. Many figures (e.g., Figures 1, 2, 5, and 6) have vertically oriented titles on the left side, which reduces readability.

2. In equation (3), just below line 198, there is a missing closing parenthesis in cos(v{n,h,w}).

final_justification.value: I have reviewed the authors’ response and read the comments from the other reviewers. Overall, I believe that if MVShoes is publicly released, it will contribute to the field. However, it should be noted that I still find the results for the shoe series style variations limited, and the accuracy in the sock region insufficient. Reviewer NYQo also pointed out that the paper should further provide real-world results on data that do not come from the authors' own dataset. Based on this, I maintain my original score of 4: Borderline accept.

title.value: ShoeFit: A New Dataset and Dual-image-stream DiT Framework for Virtual Footwear Try-On

abstract.value:
Virtual footwear try-on (VFTON), a critical yet underexplored area in virtual try-on (VTON), aims to synthesize faithful try-on results given diverse footwear and model images while maintaining 3D consistency and texture authenticity. 

Unlike conventional garment-focused VTON methods, VFTON presents unique challenges due to (1) Data Scarcity, which arises from the difficulty of perfectly matching product shoes with models wearing the identical ones, (2) Viewpoint Misalignment, where the target foot pose and source shoe views are always misaligned, leading to incomplete texture information and detail distortion, and (3) Background-induced Color Distortion, where complex material of footwear interacts with environmental lighting, causing unintended color contamination. 

To address these challenges, we introduce MVShoes, a multi-view shoe try-on dataset consisting of 7305 well-annotated image triplets, covering diverse footwear categories and challenging try-on scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a dual-stream DiT architecture, ShoeFit, designed to mitigate viewpoint misalignment through Multi-View Conditioning with 3D Rotary Position Embedding, and alleviate background-induced distortion using the LayeredRefAttention which leverages background features to modulate footwear latents. The proposed framework effectively decouples shoe appearance from environmental interferences while preserving high-quality texture detail through decoupled denoising and conditioning branches. 

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method substantially improves rendering fidelity and robustness under challenging real-world product shoes, establishing a new benchmark in high-fidelity footwear try-on synthesis. The dataset and benchmark will be publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
